{{Short description|Process in linear algebra}}
{{Use American English|date = February 2019}}

In [[linear algebra]], the '''Schmidt decomposition''' (named after its originator [[Erhard Schmidt]]) refers to a particular way of expressing a [[Coordinate vector|vector]] in the [[tensor product]] of two [[inner product space]]s. It has numerous applications in [[quantum information theory]], for example in [[quantum entanglement|entanglement]] characterization and in [[purification of quantum state|state purification]], and [[Plasticity (physics)|plasticity]].

==Theorem==
Let <math>H_1</math> and <math>H_2</math> be [[Hilbert spaces]] of [[dimension]]s ''n'' and ''m'' respectively. Assume <math>n \geq m</math>. For any vector <math>w</math> in the tensor product <math>H_1 \otimes H_2</math>, there exist orthonormal sets <math>\{ u_1, \ldots, u_m \} \subset H_1</math> and <math>\{ v_1, \ldots, v_m \} \subset H_2</math> such that <math display="inline">w= \sum_{i =1} ^m \alpha _i u_i \otimes v_i</math>, where the scalars <math>\alpha_i</math> are real, non-negative, and unique up to re-ordering.

===Proof===
The Schmidt decomposition is essentially a restatement of the [[singular value decomposition]] in a different context. Fix orthonormal bases <math>\{ e_1, \ldots, e_n \} \subset H_1</math> and <math>\{ f_1, \ldots, f_m \} \subset H_2</math>. We can identify an elementary tensor <math>e_i \otimes f_j</math> with the matrix <math>e_i f_j ^\mathsf{T}</math>, where <math>f_j ^\mathsf{T}</math> is the [[transpose]] of <math>f_j</math>. A general element of the tensor product

:<math>w = \sum _{1 \leq i \leq n, 1 \leq j \leq m} \beta _{ij} e_i \otimes f_j</math>

can then be viewed as the ''n'' × ''m'' matrix

:<math>\; M_w = (\beta_{ij}) .</math>

By the [[singular value decomposition]], there exist an ''n'' × ''n'' unitary ''U'', ''m'' × ''m'' unitary ''V'', and a [[Positive-semidefinite matrix|positive semidefinite]] diagonal ''m'' × ''m'' matrix Σ such that

:<math>M_w = U \begin{bmatrix} \Sigma \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} V^* .</math>

Write <math>U =\begin{bmatrix} U_1 & U_2 \end{bmatrix}</math> where <math>U_1</math> is ''n'' × ''m'' and we have

:<math>\; M_w = U_1 \Sigma V^* .</math>

Let <math>\{ u_1, \ldots, u_m \}</math> be the ''m'' column vectors of <math>U_1</math>, <math>\{ v_1, \ldots, v_m \}</math> the column vectors of ''<math>\overline{V}</math>'', and <math>\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_m</math> the diagonal elements of Σ. The previous expression is then

:<math>M_w = \sum _{k=1} ^m \alpha_k u_k v_k ^\mathsf{T} ,</math>

Then

:<math>w = \sum _{k=1} ^m \alpha_k u_k \otimes v_k ,</math>

which proves the claim.

==Some observations==
Some properties of the Schmidt decomposition are of physical interest.

===Spectrum of reduced states===
Consider a vector <math> w </math> of the tensor product
:<math>H_1 \otimes H_2</math>

in the form of Schmidt decomposition

:<math>w = \sum_{i =1} ^m \alpha _i u_i \otimes v_i.</math>

Form the rank 1 matrix <math> \rho = w w^* </math>. Then the [[partial trace]] of <math> \rho </math>, with respect to either system ''A'' or ''B'', is a [[diagonal matrix]] whose non-zero diagonal elements are <math> | \alpha_i|^2 </math>. In other words, the Schmidt decomposition shows that the reduced states of <math> \rho </math> on either subsystem have the same spectrum.

===Schmidt rank and entanglement===
The strictly positive values ''<math>\alpha_i</math>'' in the Schmidt decomposition of <math> w </math> are its '''Schmidt coefficients''', or '''Schmidt numbers'''.  The total number of Schmidt coefficients of <math>w</math>, counted with multiplicity, is called its '''Schmidt rank'''.

If <math> w </math> can be expressed as a product
:<math>u \otimes v</math>
then <math> w </math> is called a [[separable state]]. Otherwise, <math> w </math> is said to be an [[quantum entanglement|entangled state]]. From the Schmidt decomposition, we can see that <math> w </math> is entangled if and only if <math> w </math> has Schmidt rank strictly greater than 1.  Therefore, two subsystems that partition a [[Quantum state|pure state]] are entangled if and only if their reduced states are mixed states.

===Von Neumann entropy===

A consequence of the above comments is that, for pure states, the [[von Neumann entropy]] of the reduced states is a well-defined measure of [[quantum entanglement|entanglement]].  For the von Neumann entropy of both reduced states of <math> \rho </math> is <math display="inline">-\sum_i |\alpha_i|^2 \log\left(|\alpha_i|^2\right)</math>, and this is zero if and only if <math> \rho </math> is a product state (not entangled).

== Schmidt-rank vector ==
The Schmidt rank is defined for bipartite systems, namely quantum states

<math>|\psi\rangle \in H_A \otimes H_B</math>

The concept of Schmidt rank can be extended to quantum systems made up of more than two subsystems.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Huber|first1=Marcus|last2=de Vicente|first2=Julio I.|date=2013-01-14|title=Structure of Multidimensional Entanglement in Multipartite Systems|url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.110.030501|journal=Physical Review Letters|language=en|volume=110|issue=3|article-number=030501|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.110.030501|pmid=23373906|arxiv=1210.6876|bibcode=2013PhRvL.110c0501H|s2cid=44848143|issn=0031-9007}}</ref>

Consider the tripartite quantum system:

<math>|\psi\rangle \in H_A \otimes H_B \otimes H_C</math>

There are three ways to reduce this to a bipartite system by performing the [[partial trace]] with respect to <math>H_A, H_B</math> or <math>H_C</math>

<math>\begin{cases}
\hat{\rho}_A = Tr_A(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\\
\hat{\rho}_B = Tr_B(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\\
\hat{\rho}_C = Tr_C(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)
\end{cases}</math>

Each of the systems obtained is a bipartite system and therefore can be characterized by one number (its Schmidt rank), respectively <math>r_A, r_B</math> and <math>r_C</math>. These numbers capture the "amount of entanglement" in the bipartite system when respectively A, B or C are discarded. For these reasons the tripartite system can be described by a vector, namely the Schmidt-rank vector

<math>\vec{r} = (r_A, r_B, r_C)</math>

=== [[Multipartite entanglement|Multipartite systems]] ===
The concept of Schmidt-rank vector can be likewise extended to systems made up of more than three subsystems through the use of [[tensor]]s.

=== Example  ===
Source:<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Krenn|first1=Mario|last2=Malik|first2=Mehul|last3=Fickler|first3=Robert|last4=Lapkiewicz|first4=Radek|last5=Zeilinger|first5=Anton|date=2016-03-04|title=Automated Search for new Quantum Experiments|url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.116.090405|journal=Physical Review Letters|language=en|volume=116|issue=9|article-number=090405|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.116.090405|pmid=26991161|arxiv=1509.02749|bibcode=2016PhRvL.116i0405K|s2cid=20182586|issn=0031-9007}}</ref>

Take the tripartite quantum state <math>|\psi_{4, 2, 2}\rangle = \frac{1}{2}\big(|0, 0, 0\rangle + |1, 0, 1\rangle + |2, 1, 0\rangle + |3, 1, 1\rangle  \big)</math>

This kind of system is made possible by encoding the value of a [[qudit]] into the [[Orbital angular momentum of light|orbital angular momentum (OAM)]] of a photon rather than its [[Spin (physics)|spin]], since the latter can only take two values.

The Schmidt-rank vector for this quantum state is <math>(4, 2, 2)</math>.
